name: Ghost Button
propertyCopy: Set the button’s size, content, corners and label.
guide: Component Guide Human View Machine View Overview Ghost Button has no fill and no border at rest, only a background or color change on hover or focus - built for toolbars, cards, and dense layouts that already provide their own visual structure, so the button doesn't need one of its own. When to Use Toolbar and icon-adjacent actions - close, dismiss, expand/collapse controls. Actions inside an already-bordered container - a card, a table row, a panel header - where a second border would be redundant. Repeated per-item actions - row-level actions in a list or table where many buttons appear at once. When Not to Use A screen's main or only call to action - use Primary - Ghost is built to blend in, which works against being noticed. Anywhere the action needs to be found at a glance - use Secondary or Tertiary if some visual weight is still needed. A standalone destructive action with no surrounding context - pair Ghost with Destructive styling only when the container already makes the risk clear. Best Practices Use it inside layouts that already have visual containment (cards, toolbars, table rows) rather than as a floating standalone control. Always keep a visible hover/focus background change, since the rest state is intentionally blank. Pair with an icon when the label alone would be too subtle to notice. Do and Don't Do ✕ An icon-only dismiss action on a light or media background, where a filled button would fight the content behind it. Don't GhostGhostGhost A whole row of Ghost buttons on a plain background has almost no contrast to separate one target from the next - the row reads as one smear rather than three choices.Read More Accessibility Hover and focus states must supply a real background or outline change - a Ghost button relying on color-only text change fails WCAG 2.2's non-text contrast guidance. Still a native <button> element, fully keyboard operable. Icon-only Ghost buttons need an accessible label (aria-label or visually hidden text), since there is no visible text to announce.
